analysis.one_liner: Bans contracts requiring workers to pay union fees as a job condition.
analysis.headline: The National Right-to-Work Act drew 117 Republican cosponsors but never received a hearing or a vote, and died in committee when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite two federal labor laws to outlaw union security agreements nationwide. Today, in roughly half the states, a contract between a union and an employer can require every covered employee to pay fees to the union that bargains for them, even if the worker does not join. The bill would bar that in every workplace, including for railroad and airline employees, making union dues and fees strictly voluntary everywhere [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who choose not to join a union but work under a union contract would keep the money they would otherwise pay in fees. Employers would gain over time as unions collect less money and shrink, weakening the bargaining power that negotiates pay and working conditions [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Amends the National Labor Relations Act to strike the provisions that let a union contract require employees to pay dues or fees as a condition of employment [S2] [S3].
Amends the Railway Labor Act to strike the provision letting rail carriers require payroll deduction of union dues as a job condition, covering railroad and airline workers [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Unions would lose the fee income from workers they must represent, and workers in unionized workplaces would bear the indirect cost: in states with these laws, unions are smaller and, by most studies, pay and benefits are lower than in states that allow fee requirements [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a free-rider problem: unions would still be legally required to represent every worker in the bargaining unit, including those who pay nothing, while losing the money that pays for representation [S2] [S3].

Research on states with right-to-work laws consistently finds lower wages, lower benefits, and weaker union membership compared with states that allow union fee agreements, so the bill's individual-choice framing comes at a measurable cost to covered workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a real individual benefit — no worker is forced to fund an organization they choose not to join — but stacks it against the financial foundation of collective bargaining. The national economic evidence on right-to-work states points to lower pay for union and non-union workers alike, so the trade-off as designed favors employers more than workers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to a subcommittee in April 2013, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Steve King (R-IA) introduced the National Right-to-Work Act on March 5, 2013 [S1] [S3].
117 House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did [S4].

The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day of introduction, and on April 23, 2013, to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions, where it stayed for the rest of the Congress [S5].
No further action was taken, and the bill expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Unions and workers in unionized workplaces kept the existing fee system and the union finances it supports. Employers who would have benefited from smaller, weaker unions gained nothing from this outcome.

for.name: Rep. Steve King
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 57 initial Republican cosponsors [S3].

for.name: 117 of 234 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it an all-Republican effort [S4].

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee (Chair John Kline)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or brought the bill forward after referral; it sat at the subcommittee level for the rest of the Congress [S5].

against.name: Labor unions (AFL-CIO and affiliated unions)
against.what_they_did: Opposed national right-to-work legislation, which would cut the fee revenue unions collect from workers they are required to represent.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the 117 cosponsors was a Republican and no Democrat signed on [S4].

industries.note: The bill would bar unions from collecting fees from workers they must represent, cutting their funding nationwide. Unions use that money to bargain for higher pay and benefits, but the fee mandate is also the reason some workers resent them.

With unions collecting less and shrinking, employers would face weaker bargaining counterparts and lower labor costs. The gain to employers comes directly from the reduced bargaining power that supports workers' wages.
